data.title: Corn (clavus) — viva
data.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Corn (clavus)** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is a corn?**
- Sharply circumscribed, painful hyperkeratotic lesion with a central translucent, conical keratin core (radix) that presses on underlying dermal nerves; due to localised repeated pressure over bony prominences

**Q2. Types.**
- Hard corn (heloma durum): dorsolateral fifth toe, tops of interphalangeal joints (claw/hammer toes), sole over metatarsal heads
- Soft corn (heloma molle): macerated white lesion in the interdigital space (commonly 4th web) from opposing bony prominences — may be mistaken for tinea pedis
- Seed corns (heloma miliare): multiple tiny corns on weight-bearing sole
- Vascular and neurofibrous corns (painful, bleeding on paring)

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Plantar wart (black dots, interrupted skin lines, pain on lateral pressure), callus, punctate keratoderma, porokeratosis plantaris discreta, foreign body, eccrine poroma, tinea pedis/soft corn

**Q4. Paring test.**
- Paring a corn reveals a central translucent core with intact skin lines; paring a wart shows pinpoint bleeding black dots and interrupted dermatoglyphics

**Q5. Management.**
- Relieve pressure: wide-toed shoes, corn pads/doughnut cushions, toe separators (soft corn), orthotics, correct toe deformities (surgery for persistent cases — exostectomy, arthroplasty)
- Paring/enucleation of the core with a scalpel — immediate relief
- Keratolytic plasters (salicylic acid 40%), urea creams; avoid caustic corn caps in diabetics/peripheral vascular disease
- Recurrence common unless mechanical cause corrected

**Q6. Histopathology of a corn.**
- Cup-shaped depression of the epidermis filled with a dense central column of parakeratotic keratin (the core) pressing into the dermis; surrounding hyperkeratosis; thinned granular layer beneath the core

**Q7. Why are corns painful?**
- The central keratin core (inverted cone) presses on dermal nerve endings and bursa over a bony prominence; soft corns can macerate and become infected

**Q8. Where do soft corns occur and why?**
- Between toes (usually 4th web space) where a bony prominence (condyle of proximal phalanx) presses on the adjacent toe; moisture keeps them soft and white (macerated); may mimic interdigital tinea

**Q9. What surgical or orthopaedic options exist for recurrent corns?**
- Correct underlying deformity — exostectomy, condylectomy, hammer-toe correction; silicone toe separators and padding; avoid tight pointed footwear

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful circumscribed lesion with central translucent core over bony prominence — corn
- Soft corn in 4th toe web

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mechanical injuries). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
